verses.zh: 法老攻击迦萨之先，有耶和华论非利士人的话临到先知耶利米。
verses.en: This was[NOTE:1] the Lord’s message to the prophet Jeremiah about the Philistines before Pharaoh attacked Gaza:[NOTE:2]
notes: The precise dating of this prophecy is uncertain. Several proposals have been suggested, the most likely of which is that the prophecy was delivered in 609 b.c. in conjunction with Pharaoh Necho’s advance into Palestine to aid the Assyrians. That was the same year Josiah was killed by Necho at the battle of Megiddo and four years before Necho was defeated by Nebuchadnezzar, the foe from the north. The prophecy presupposes that Ashkelon is still in existence (v. 5); hence it must be before 604 b.c. For a fairly complete discussion of the options see G. L. Keown, P. J. Scalise, T. G. Smothers, Jeremiah 26-52 (WBC), 299-300.
verses.commentary:
47:1 This first verse dates the prophecy (i.e. "before Pharaoh conquered Gaza"). There are
several other places where the destruction of Philistia is prophesied (cf. Isa. 14:29-31; Ezek. 25:15-17;
Joel 3:4-8; Amos 1:6-8; Zeph. 2:4-7; Zech 9:5-7).

Herodotus (Hist. II, 159) mentions that Pharaoh Necho II conquered a Philistine city
(i.e. Gaza) about 609 B.C. This would link up with his replacing Josiah's heir (Jehoahaz)
with another puppet king (Jehoiakim), also in 609 B.C. The problem with this date is that
Nebuchadnezzar II did not invade until 601 B.C.

The Expositors Bible Commentary, vol. 6, p. 655, lists three possible dates for the
invasion of Neo-Babylon (if the MT is correct).

- 609 B.C. ‒ same time as the death of Josiah by Necho II

- 604 B.C. ‒ after the defeat of the Egyptian army at Carchemish

- still later in the reign of Pharaoh Hophra (or Apries, 588-569 B.C.), when he
invaded Phoenicia and Philistia, which were on the way (i.e. southern coast)

verses.zh: 耶和华如此说：有水从北方发起，成为涨溢的河，要涨过遍地和其中所有的，并城和其中所住的。人必呼喊；境内的居民都必哀号。
verses.en: “Look! Enemies are gathering in the north like water rising in a river.[NOTE:1] They will be like an overflowing stream.They will overwhelm the whole country and everything in it like a flood.They will overwhelm the cities and their inhabitants.People will cry out in alarm.Everyone living in the country will cry out in pain.
notes: Heb “Behold! Waters are rising from the north.” The metaphor of enemy armies compared to overflowing water occurs also in Isa 8:8-9 (Assyria) and 46:7-8 (Egypt). Here it refers to the foe from the north (Jer 1:14; 4:6; etc), which is specifically identified with Babylon in Jer 25. The metaphor has been turned into a simile in the translation to help the average reader identify that a figure is involved, and to hint at the referent.
verses.commentary:
47:2 "waters. . .from the north" The invasion of Neo-Babylon into Palestine has been
characterized by several images.

- overflowing boiling pot pouring south (cf. Jer. 1:13-14)

- biting fly from the north (cf. Jer. 46:20)

- here as a flooding river (Egypt is often described as the flooding Nile)

The imagery of an invading nation as an overflowing river is common in the OT.

- Assyria ‒ Isa. 8:8-9

- Egypt ‒ Jer. 46:7-8; Amos 8:8; 9:5

47:2e-3 This describes the actions of the Philistines.

- the men cry out, Jer. 47:2e

- every inhabitant of the land will wail, Jer. 47:2f

- fathers have not turned back for their children, Jer. 47:3c

- their hands are limp, Jer. 47:3d

What has terrified them?

- the noise of the galloping hooves of his stallions, Jer. 47:3a

- the tumult of his chariots, Jer. 47:3b

verses.zh: 听见敌人壮马蹄跳的响声和战车隆隆、车轮轰轰；为父的手就发软，不回头看顾儿女。
verses.en: Fathers will hear the hoofbeats of the enemies’ horses,the clatter of their chariots and the rumbling of their wheels.They will not turn back to save their childrenbecause they will be paralyzed with fear.[NOTE:1]
notes: Heb “From the noise of the stamping of the hoofs of his stallions, from the rattling of his chariots at the rumbling of their wheels, fathers will not turn to their children from sinking of hands.” According to BDB 952 s.v. רִפָּיוֹן, the “sinking of the hands” is figurative of helplessness caused by terror. A very similar figure appears with a related expression in Isa 35:3-4. The sentence has been restructured to put the subject up front and to suggest the same causal connections through shorter sentences more in keeping with contemporary English style. The figures have been interpreted for the sake of clarity for the average reader.

verses.zh: 因为日子将到，要毁灭一切非利士人，剪除帮助泰尔、西顿所剩下的人。原来耶和华必毁灭非利士人，就是迦斐托海岛余剩的人。
verses.en: For the time has come to destroy all the Philistines.The time has come to destroy all the helpthat remains for Tyre[NOTE:1] and Sidon.[NOTE:2] For I, the Lord, will[NOTE:3] destroy the Philistines,that remnant that came from the island of Crete.[NOTE:4]
notes: For location see Map1-A2; Map2-G2; Map4-A1; JP3-F3; JP4-F3.
For location see Map1-A1; JP3-F3; JP4-F3.
Heb “For the Lord will.” The first person style has been adopted because the Lord is speaking (cf. v. 2).

All the help that remains for Tyre and Sidon and that remnant that came from the island of Crete appear to be two qualifying phrases that refer to the Philistines, the last pertaining to their origin and the first to their vital alliance with Tyre and Sidon. “Crete” is literally “Caphtor,” which is generally identified with the island of Crete. The Philistines had come from there (Amos 9:7) in the wave of migration from the Aegean Islands during the twelfth and eleventh centuries. They had settled on the Philistine plain after having been repulsed from trying to enter Egypt.
verses.commentary:
47:4 All of the small nations on the Mediterranean coast (the only possible land
route from Mesopotamia to Egypt because of the desert in between) will be invaded and defeated.

▣ "The remnant of the coastland of Caphtor" The Philistines were from Caphtor
(cf. Deut. 2:23; Amos 9:7). However, "Caphtor" here may be a reference to

- all the islands of the eastern Mediterranean

- a region of northern Egypt

- the island of Crete (best guess)

- less likely, but possibly, the island of Cyprus

verses.zh: 迦萨成了光秃；平原中所剩的亚实基伦归于无有。你用刀划身，要到几时呢？
verses.en: The people of Gaza will shave their heads in mourning.The people of Ashkelon will be struck dumb.How long will you gash yourselves to show your sorrow,[NOTE:1] you who remain of Philistia’s power?[NOTE:2]
notes: Shaving one’s head and gashing one’s body were customs to show mourning or sadness for the dead (cf. Deut 14:1; Mic 1:16; Ezek 27:31; Jer 16:6; 48:37).

Or “you who are left alive on the Philistine plain.” Or “you who remain of the Anakim.” The translation follows the suggestion of several of the modern commentaries that the word עֵמֶק (ʿemeq) means “strength” or “power” here (see J. A. Thompson, Jeremiah [NICOT], 698; J. Bright, Jeremiah [AB], 310; and see also HALOT 803 s.v. II עֵמֶק). It is a rare homonym of the word that normally means “valley,” which seems to be an inappropriate designation of the Philistine plain. Many of the modern English versions and commentaries follow the Greek version, which reads here “remnant of the Anakim” (עֲנָקִים [ʿanaqim] instead of עִמְקָם [ʿimqam], a confusion of basically one letter). This emendation is followed by both BDB 771 s.v. עֵמֶק and KBL 716 s.v. עֵמֶק. The Anakim were generally associated with the southern region around Hebron, but an enclave of them was known to have settled in Gaza, Gath, and Ekron, three of the Philistine cities (cf. Josh 11:22). However, the facts that this judgment is directed against the Philistines, not the Anakim, and that this homonym apparently appears also in Jer 49:4 make the reading of “power” more likely here.
verses.commentary:
47:5 There were five independent city-states which made up Philistia (i.e. same political structure as Greece).

- Gaza

- Ashkelon

- Ashdad

- Gath

- Ekron

▣

NASB, NKJV, JPSOA
"O remnant of their valley"

NRSV
"O remnant of their power"

NJB
"you who remain in the valley"

LXX, RSV
"the remaining Enakim" (i.e. "Anakites,"

cf. Josh. 11:22)

REB, NET
"the remnant of the Philistine power"

The NASB reflects the MT.

- The NRSV and REB assume a different root found in Ugaritic (AB, p. 310).

- The REB assumes that Ashkelon was the only remaining undefeated Philistine city-state.

- The LXX is an emendation about the giants found at Gaza, Gath, and Ashdad in Josh. 11:22.

- The UBS Text Project, p. 296, gives "of the Anakim" a "C" rating (considerable doubt).

▣ "gash yourself" This was part of

- their idol worship (see SPECIAL TOPIC: FERTILITY WORSHIP OF THE ANE)

- their mourning rites (see SPECIAL TOPIC: GRIEVING RITES)

Because of the parallelism with Jer. 47:5a, probably #2 is correct.

verses.zh: 耶和华的刀剑哪，你到几时才止息呢？你要入鞘，安靖不动。
verses.en: How long will you cry out,[NOTE:1] ‘Oh, sword of the Lord,how long will it be before you stop killing?[NOTE:2] Go back into your sheath;stay there and rest!’[NOTE:3]
notes: The words “How long will you cry out” are not in the text, but some such introduction seems necessary because the rest of the speech assumes a personal subject.

The passage is highly figurative. The sword of the Lord, which is itself a figure of the destructive agency of the enemy armies, is here addressed as a person and is encouraged by rhetorical questions (questions designed to dissuade) and commands to “be quiet,” “be at rest,” and “be silent,” all of which aim to get the Lord to call off the destruction against the Philistines.
verses.commentary:
47:6 This verse addresses the personified sword of YHWH (cf. Jer. 12:12; Isa. 34:6; Amos 9:4).

The question is asked (apparently by those being conquered) how long will it

- not be quieted

- withdraw into its sheath

- be at rest

- stay still

The last three are IMPERATIVES!

verses.zh: 耶和华既吩咐你攻击亚实基伦和海边之地，他已经派定你，焉能止息呢？
verses.en: But how can it rest[NOTE:1] when I, the Lord, have[NOTE:2] given it orders?I have ordered it to attackthe people of Ashkelon and the seacoast.”[NOTE:3]
notes: The reading here follows the Greek, Syriac, and Latin versions. The Hebrew text reads, “how can you rest,” as a continuation of the second person in v. 6.
Heb “When the Lord has.” The first person is again adopted because the Lord has been speaking.

Heb “Against Ashkelon and the sea coast, there he has appointed it.” For the switch to the first person see the preceding translator’s note. “There” is poetical and redundant, and the idea of “attacking” is implicit in “against.”
verses.commentary:
47:7 Verse 7 is an answer to the question of Jer. 47:6 (i.e. LXX text). There is no rest
for YHWH's sword because the conquest of Palestine by Neo-Babylon is His will (i.e. "He has assured it,"
BDB 416, KB 419, Qal PERFECT). YHWH is in charge of world history! He now
uses Babylon, as He previously used Assyria (i.e. Isa. 10:5) and will use Persia (i.e. Isa. 44:28; 45:1-3) in
the future, to accomplish His purposes.

▣ "against Ashkelon" The IVP Bible Background Commentary (OT) has a good brief
article about this on page 679.

- From Babylonian Chronicle ‒

- Nebuchadnezzsar II attacked surprisingly in the rainy season (i.e., Kislev)

- Walls of the city were breached and the soldiers ransacked and burned the city, turning it into a mound of ruins.

- From archaeology, the date of the destruction was about 604 B.C. See Biblical Archaeology Library

- Ashkelon was a major port for Mediterranian maritime trade with Egypt. Neo-Babylon's control of Philistia was a real
problem for Egypt.

The NET Bible, p. 1424, #5, suggests that although Ashkelon was destroyed in 604 B.C., this prophecy dates from
609 B.C., in which Pharaoh Necho II marched through Judah to aid the remnant of the Assyrian army, but both Egypt and
Assyria were defeated at Carchemish in 605 B.C. by the Neo-Babylonian army.
